speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head T of the Estimates to be reduced by $100".

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The recent public housing Motion and conclusion of the Budget debate saw a very vigorous discussion in the House with the Budget providing assurances and pledging more support to ensuring affordability and accessibility to public housing.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Several Parliamentary colleagues sought more details on the support to be rendered and offering suggestions for consideration to address the intricate issue of housing affordability and accessibility on the long run.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This is a matter not just about encouraging birth rates.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Instead, it is about giving clarity to young families so they can better plan their lives around their careers, where to live after marriage and how to find the appropriate caregiving support for their children and parents as family sizes shrinks.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Many of us today have the benefit of living with our parents when we are fresh out of school and not worry about it until we are of certain age or begin our lives with our better half.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Our society now faces new demands, changing trends and aspirations whereby young adults want their own independence or shared spaces soon after graduating.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Young families requiring more space to cope with work from home and their children want to have their own rooms while growing up.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: More seniors are seeing empty nests after their children have their own homes and the seniors increasingly find it difficult to upkeep their existing homes as they age but are unsure if they can indeed enjoy the new home that they right-size to.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: So, what do we do with these changing needs?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I wish to raise a few suggestions for MND's consideration in future housing supply and new builds.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As more young families aspire to upgrade or move to larger units over time, would it not be more suitable for them to obtain a larger unit from the start and live in it for a longer period?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This way, the market demand will not increase on a cyclical basis and the minimum occupation period (MOP) can be increased to curb near term price increase which is inevitable in every sale.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Families will have more stability in anchoring their lives around a neighbourhood, as over time, there will be less distinction between mature and non-mature estates with better transportation networks and more infrastructures available in new towns.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Further, the resale market for 3-room flats can be sustained for those who require and be kept more affordable without competing with the new BTOs' supply.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Such supply builds will be done for a specified period and reviewed regularly to monitor its impact over a decade.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While there are no details around VERS now, we know that many flats built in the 1970s to early 1980s would fall in this category in the coming decade or so.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The need to shift current cohort of VERS flat owners to new flats meant more land and more new builds are required regardless of the size.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Singles and families who rent from the open market will also further add to this demand even without any significant increase in our total country's population.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Despite the trend of more singles or people marrying at a later age, singles will not form the majority of our society and people who do eventually settle down when the timing and factors are right.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Thus, the large bulk of this demand is transient and may actually better cater to the needs of those who require them for several years till they enter the next stage of their lives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Today, rental flats are only made available to the low-income group while those who wish to rent or have interim housing need to rely on flats that HDB have on hand.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Third, new variety of flats for seniors who right-size.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Today, seniors who right-size appear to have a preference for some type of flats.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Those from the private housing generally purchase 5-room or Executive Apartment (EA) resale flats and those who moved from the HDB flat would choose a 2-room Flexi or 3-room resale flats.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For seniors who are looking for flat options to right-size or to live in community assisted care apartments, is it possible for HDB to refurbish and re-configure existing blocks of flats to allow better caregiving needs and active ageing in place instead of having nursing homes?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Of course, HDB has to assess the structural stability of infrastructure and economics taken into consideration to decide if alteration of existing units or new builds of such units would make more sense.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The lower housing cost under AHS will allow Singaporeans to afford housing without depleting their Central Provident Fund (CPF) savings.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They can look forward to a comfortable retirement and no longer need to worry about the ups and downs of the resale market, the lease decay and the ever-changing policies of the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government must admit that the current housing system has reached its limits.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister has argued that the main problem is temporary short supply.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the biggest problem we face is actually ever-increasing BTO prices.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What will be the BTO price in 20 years' time?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Future generations will have to constantly worry about BTO prices.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, the AHS will ensure that every Singaporean of each generation will be able to afford an HDB flat because he pays only the construction cost and not the land cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The land cost is waived because public housing is considered a public good.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the most equitable way of distributing the benefits of our land to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The AHS also continues to offer Singaporeans the choice of making a profit from his flat by selling in the resale market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the BTO flat, it is for recouping the loan servicing cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And for the AHS flat, it is for paying the deferred land cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The deferred land cost feature prevents the AHS owner from profiteering from selling his flat.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This also prevents the AHS owners from affecting the resale market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Overwhelmed by the value proposition of the AHS, the Government has tried to frighten Singaporeans into thinking that the PSP is going to cause a crash in resale flat prices with our policy proposals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the short term, it is a policy intent of AHS to cause a slight adjustment in the current surging resale market so as to enable keen buyers to get their flats at a more reasonable price.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That will be healthy after recent market exuberance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the resale price will recover in the long term because fewer AHS owners are likely to sell as they can live in the flat throughout their life without paying for the land cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, there will also be support for the resale market from the backlog of first-timer demand.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, buyers who are ineligible for new flats, buyers who want to live in a specific location because they want to live near their parents, permanent residents and upgraders form a large pool of demand that will underpin the resale market which is still much cheaper than the private property market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The AHS will not require excessive fiscal resources to implement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most of the land cost forgone at the beginning is recoverable from the deferred land cost later.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Effectively, we will only defer our reserved accumulation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans may ask if all these are too good to be true and where is the caveat.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And all these are possible because the Government has acquired the land from the 1970s to the 1980s at zero or nominal cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We only need our rich "ah gong" to agree to do more for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: However, could the Ministry share its assessment of whether or how this might drive up resale prices even more.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I know the Ministry has put out the statement and Deputy Prime Minister Wong has also touched on this in his round-up speech in the Budget debate.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But could the Ministry share a fuller assessment?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: HDB retail shop fronts near commercial centres close to MRT stations and major infrastructure enjoy high footfall.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The same cannot be said for all HDB retail shops, particularly those in smaller or more isolated HDB commercial areas.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Today, however, it is not uncommon to see this particular rule generally disregarded with some ODAs rented and sublet out to itinerant traders for a few hours each day.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would imagine that one of the ostensible purposes for HDB Commercial department to establish the rule against the display of dissimilar ODA goods would be to ensure that there is not an excess of one type of trade in the area where a broad range of goods and services are usually available.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For their part, Town Councils extend the use of ODA to shopkeepers and lessees and have powers to revoke ODAs if necessary.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When such powers are used in keeping with the spirit of the HDB Commercial rule that ODAs are only to be used for the display of similar trade items that are found in the shops, some itinerant traders and the lessees or owners of the shops that sublet their ODA questioned why such rules are not enforced in other commercial areas where they operate as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does the HDB entertain exceptions to the aforesaid rules that can be sought with the approval of the HDB Commercial section to allow itinerant traders to sell their goods at the ODAs?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, in view of a possible imbalance of shops in a typical area or because of the limited variety of shops in a commercial area or simply to encourage vibrancy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would be grateful for some clarity in this regard.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The rents for these shops tend to be lower than those at shopping centres and the shops are often run by residents who live around there or are familiar faces.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It adds vibrancy, character and identity to the place.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is important to keep the barrier to entry low in these heartland locations so that entrepreneurship can flourish in these neighbourhood settings and also serve the local community and beyond.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I ask what is the Ministry of National Development (MND) or HDB's thinking on encouraging innovative startups as well as social enterprises to set up at heartland commercial precincts?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: To do this, we also need to further refresh the shop spaces in the heartlands.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: If yes, can I take this opportunity to also register my interest for Bukit Panjang?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have a vibrant heartland market at Bangkit and it is most ideal for an enhanced ROS.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The rising cost of living and uncertain economic outlook have made Singaporeans more cost conscious about their food options, which makes hawker centres, with their eclectic mix of delicious local food at affordable prices, the preferred places for meals for most.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, given the uneven distribution of hawker centres around Singapore, some Singaporeans are, unfortunately, disadvantaged on this front.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There is no real justification for some locations having a lot more hawker centres than others.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As they are a key feature of Singapore’s unique culture and heritage and are Singaporeans’ preferred daily go-to place for affordable food, they should be built in every town centre.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hawker centres, like HDB shops, not only make heartland living vibrant, they also support small local businesses run by and employing residents living nearby.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Pioneering hawkers should be charged lower rents prior to demand building up and reassessed based on traffic and tenants' sales progress.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would be fair to the first few batches of residents and hawkers in new towns.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Stall leases should be awarded on the basis of retail diversity and the range of prices, among others.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In my HDB (Amendment) Bill speech earlier this year, I called for the Government to not forget neighbourhoods, such as Sengkang, which do not have the benefit of the convenience and rich diversity of having heartland shops in close proximity to our homes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As advised by Senior Minister of State Sim Ann back then, I had since written to HDB on this matter and I look forward to hearing from HDB and working closely with the team on the low retail and food options within the existing precincts of Sengkang.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan, your three cuts together, please.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Could MND do more to attract startups to set up shops in our heartland commercial precincts?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Also, under the current Social Enterprise Scheme, HDB offers commercial spaces at subsidised rent to raise registered social enterprises.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Could MND update on the uptake and does it have plans to further enhance the initiative?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I can imagine, too, a broader youth‐driven microeconomy in each of our HDB neighbourhoods, if we can couple these heartland enterprises with co‐living facilities in the heartlands and allow youths working in the heartlands to also play and live together.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And HDB does not have to do this by itself.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How had noted, there is, today, a vibrant market with multiple commercial players.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, HDB can partner private operators, but set standards, including in pricing and affordability, and take the lead in developing the market for essentially short-term flexible rental for youths by way of co‐living arrangements in heartland locations.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To be clear, I think the current eligible age for singles for both BTO and resale flats is appropriate and should remain.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Nonetheless, we can do more to help singles 35 and above to own their BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This would likely increase the overall demand for 3-room BTOs, but it is part of evolving our balance and, to strike a balance, we could preserve the supply currently set aside for first‐timer families.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Chairman, in my cut last year, I called for the Government to build a larger percentage of HDB stock ahead of demand.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: We all recognise that long waiting times are not just an inconvenience but seriously affect Singaporeans’ life plans, such as causing young couples to delay starting a family.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Someone shared with me a blog post by a certain Prof Ben Leong which I agree with, and I quote, “Having excess flats is actually a feature and not a bug.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: It just means that if some Singaporeans want to get married and want a new house straightaway, there is a house available!”, and he goes on further to say, “To me, BTO is the real culprit behind our uncontrolled fire”.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Most importantly, any such risk of marginal excess supply would be worthwhile taking to achieve the social need to reduce average BTO wait times and, in turn, support Singaporeans in charting their lives and starting new families.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, communes and co-living are housing formats where people come together to live, share their resources and responsibilities for fostering mutual support .

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We can optimise our land used for housing with these two concepts.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: An example is “mommune” – a commune for mums.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This model exists in both Japan and Hong Kong where single mothers and their children live together as a large communal family.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: They pool their domestic and childcare-related resources to reduce the economic burdens of single parenthood.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: By splitting chores, finances and babysitting duties, single parents have more bandwidth to explore enriching experiences to benefit their children.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We should explore this model and apply it to other groups which need extra support to manage their day-to-day lives, such as families with special needs children and members who are persons with disability.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Co-living apartments can be built for people to have their own private rooms but share common spaces, such as pantry, kitchen, living room and laundry space.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This creates physical social interaction opportunities for a generation of people who have grown more used to online interaction.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: For all we know, it may also improve our marriage rates!

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Private companies, such as Hamlet and Cove, already offer co-living options near the city, albeit at a premium price.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Why not have it available as public housing, too, for young adults to access lower priced housing on short leases, while living amongst their peer groups with similar lifestyle preferences?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, we can co-locate these singles’ precincts with community care apartments for the elderly and communes for various needs families – creating convenient opportunities for them to volunteer near their homes.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Ground-up initiatives, in the likes of Kampung Kakis and SG Assist, have shown that Singaporeans love to help out and they love to help out conveniently.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I urge the Government agencies working on this project to explore these suggestions and consult interested Singaporeans with relevant experience in these fields to advance these ideas.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Chairman, in November last year, I asked the Minister for National Development if the funds obtained by HDB to issue housing loans are derived from CPF and whether the Government can consider to unpeg the HDB concessionary interest rate for housing loans from the prevailing CPF Ordinary Account (OA) interest rate and, if not, why not.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I understand the rationale for the HDB to impose a spread of 0.10% above the OA rate to recover HDB’s cost of administering loans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: But the bigger issue is, rather than being dogmatic about pegging the HDB concessionary interest rate at 0.10% above the prevailing CPF OA interest rate, can MOF and, in turn, HDB and MND not make the call to segregate the two distinct roles of the OA savings rate and the HDB loan rate?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Singaporeans are rightly concerned that if the OA rates do somehow rise in future, then there could be higher home loan rates as well, given this peg.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: However, given that MND has made it abundantly clear that the funds obtained by HDB to issue housing loans are from the Development Fund, not CPF, can we not let the concerns around the home loan peg hold us back from the correct decision of providing for both mortgage stability and certainty and also retirement adequacy for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Chairman, MND has a variety of policies – proximity housing grants, affordable neighborhood centres, affordable interest rates – that contribute to an affordable cost of living for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Nevertheless, we are experiencing a prolonged increase in cost of living over the last few years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Are there more that MND, in concert with other Ministries, can use to do mitigate rising prices?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For example, HDB has modified the criterion for selecting coffee shop operators in recent years, where affordable pricing is also an important consideration.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Can HDB share more about the success of this initiative, and whether more can be done for other HDB shops?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Is there more that HDB can do to ensure that HDB interest rates remain affordable and that more Singaporeans, especially freelancers, platform workers as well as micro-SME owners, can benefit from HDB's low interest rates?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And can HDB share whether there are any additional plans to manage cost of living?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, loan delinquency provides another angle to look at affordability.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Specifically, in the past three years, with breakdown by flat type, how many HDB flats were behind in payments, how many were eventually taken back by HDB and, for those flats taken back by HDB, what is the maximum and minimum number of months they have been in arrears and where are the families staying now?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Were they settled in rental flats or other shelters?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How much of their earlier payments do they get back?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do they get back the full amount paid plus accrued interest?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, in my Budget debate speech, I talked about the sentiments of young first-timer applicants and how we can tweak the HDB balloting process to achieve equitable outcomes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need to provide affordable and accessible housing to all segments of society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How is HDB going to help first-timers starting their families and first-timers with children to achieve a better chance at securing a BTO flat?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On seniors, how many seniors have successfully taken up the Silver Housing Bonus (SHB) and how is MND going to continue supporting seniors looking to right-size and monetise their flats?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Back in January this year, I asked MND whether the Government would consider providing a time-limited rental subsidy for rental flat applicants who qualify for the Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme (PPHS) and Public Rental Scheme (PRS) respectively, provided that they are unable to find alternative temporary housing arrangements and have been unsuccessful in obtaining a flat from HDB after a pre-defined time period.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: In the replies to many of my residents’ unsuccessful appeals to HDB, the open market appears to be HDB’s catch-all solution to those who have been unsuccessful in meeting their housing needs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Whether it is for those who qualify for, but are unsuccessful in obtaining a PPHS or PRS, those who are lucky enough to qualify for one but face long wait times or those who are not successful or successful in their BTO flat application.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Yet, for various reasons, largely relating to the current demand and supply situation, open market rentals have continued to soar, and are increasingly out of many Singaporeans’ budgets.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: As it is, the qualifying criteria for the PPHS and PRS schemes are very stringent.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: So, I do hope the Government can reconsider my suggestion to maintain open market rental affordability.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Public Rental Scheme (PRS) provides a roof over the heads of Singaporeans who have problems affording their own homes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would MND share an update on the Joint Singles Scheme-Operator Run (JSS-OR) pilot that was launched at the end of 2021 to provide an addition option to the Joint Singles Scheme (JSS) for single persons?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How effective has this scheme been so far?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During last month’s debates on HDB housing, it was acknowledged by MND that some families were not ready to buy HDB flats as they first needed to build up their finances.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are also other families who used to own flats, but due to disruptions such as divorce or business failure, ended up losing their homes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: HDB rental housing is a valued option for such families and individuals.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From what I have seen from my Meet-the-People Sessions, the demand for rental housing is very high.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: HDB’s eligibility criteria for rental flats are understandably strict.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singles must be aged 35 or older before they can apply to co-share with another tenant.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From my observations, these parameters lead to hardship on two fronts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A household earning above $1,500 to say, $2,500 may not be able to afford other housing options.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for purchasing a flat, much depends on one’s CPF savings, age and ability to work.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Though the flats may be small, this does not translate into smaller household sizes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The small size of flats means that families may be not able to confine their belongings to the unit itself, resulting in possessions being placed along the common corridors, affecting the living environment and becoming potential fire hazards.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I note that HDB’s recent initiatives to improve living conditions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It has been announced that there will be improvements in lighting and ventilation of new rental blocks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A separate initiative proposes to mix rental flats with owner-occupied flats.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These are welcome moves and I hope the Government will continue to look for ways to both improve the quality of rental housing and reduce the stigma of living in the rental flats.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Related to this, I would like to ask two questions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are some of the feedback received and lessons from the scheme, as well as who the main applicants to the scheme have been, for example, are they seniors?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If so, what proportions of flats under JSS will be allocated to this and on what timeline?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Additionally, families who are sometimes caught in limbo as they eagerly await their BTO keys have turned to the Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme (PPHS).

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could HDB provide an update on whether application rates have further fallen or remain high, and if the proportion of individuals who were offered a flat but eventually rejected them has decreased?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are four schemes under PRS: Family Scheme, ComLink Rental Scheme, Joint Singles Scheme and Joint Singles Scheme Operator-Run (JSS-OR) Pilot.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How does HDB apportion the number of flats to each of the four schemes under PRS?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does HDB prioritise applications where there are children involved?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Has HDB received more applications for these flats in recent months?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The increasing rental rates in the open market would have made it more challenging for those who are renting.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the general increase in pay, would the household income cap of $1,500 be reviewed?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will HDB also share an update on the Joint Singles Scheme Operator-Run (JSS-OR) Pilot rolled out in end-2021, where HDB helps to match flat mates based on their common factors?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is meant as an alternative to the Joint Singles Scheme.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How many were in HDB flats and does MND have a breakdown of flat types, including public rental flats?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If public rental and smaller flats account for more of the fires, would the Ministry consider more targeted public education programmes to increase awareness of fire safety and prevention?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Timely reminders and advisories can potentially save lives.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would HDB also consider including the Home Fire Alarm Device (HFAD) as an essential item under the Home Improvement Programme’s (HIP) - Essential Improvements scheme?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While there is no correlation to indicate the fire cases were due to age of flats, the installation of HFAD would help in response time if such fires were to occur within the flat.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could SCDF share information on the causes of fires following the investigations with the relevant agencies such as HDB and Town Council for knowledge management?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Ministry consider subsidising comprehensive fire insurance for lower-income families?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If HDB can act as a “bulk” insurance purchaser with co-payments from these households, the negotiated premiums would likely be much more affordable.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the recent debate over public housing, I appealed to HDB to invest more resources to build flats faster to catch up on the time lost due to the COVID-19. pandemic.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is vital to shorten the waiting times for BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: HDB should continue to work with the construction sector to utilise new and faster building techniques to reduce time for completion of projects.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will naturally increase the supply of flats in the market to alleviate supply and demand pressures and moderate price increases as the competition for resale flats is lowered.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the COS debate last year, I spoke on adopting the Prefabricated Prefinished Volumetric Construction (PPVC) method more widely to improve building productivity.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With constraints on skilled manpower, increased productivity through better technological solutions is key to building our flats faster.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides PPVC, what other forms of Design for Manufacturing and Assembly (DfMA), where some construction work is moved off-site into factories to prefabricate building modules, are utilised for the construction of our HDB flats?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Integrated Digital Delivery (IDD) is another way to boost productivity, whereby all stakeholders involved in a building project collaborate through digital platforms.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Productivity Innovation Project (PIP) and the Productivity Solutions Grant (PSG) are two of the schemes under the Construction Productivity and Capability Fund.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Companies can also apply for the PSG, which co-funds up to 70% of the cost of adopting off-the-shelf digital solutions.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would MND share what are the take-up rates of these schemes and how they have translated into expediting the building of our HDB flats?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: HDB declined to redesignate the MSCP space for coffee shops or cloud kitchens, but many MSCPs remain under-utilised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More and more families are purchasing bicycles in pursuit of healthy lifestyles, but face parking constraints.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Delivery riders also find little space to park while making drop-offs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I propose that we redesignate the ground floor of under-utilised MSCPs for bike and delivery parking and shift vehicle parking one floor up.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Since my speech, I have noted several other potential misalignments with HDB and other agencies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Another example is the installation of automated fire rated roller shutters in carparks of new BTO flats due to a design consequence: the siting of a carpark near a substation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This in turn will have an effect on cost of living, notwithstanding the S&CC grants.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I invite the hon Minister’s views on this.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Chair, coffee shops and eating houses are familiar features in our neighbourhoods, providing a selection of warm meals to residents after a long day at work or school.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: They also provide a respite to the frail elderly, homemakers and caregivers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Considering inflationary pressures, would MND share how it will ensure the affordability of these important meal options at the eateries in our heartlands?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This House has just debated that HDB (Amendment) Bill in January where my Sengkang teammate Louis Chua spoke about the disparity in the number of coffee shops typically found in mature estates versus relatively new ones such as Sengkang.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Today, I wish to speak about not so much the difference in quality but also the difference in price faced by our residents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: One reason for this is that there are simply less coffee shops and hawker centres in newer estates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Hawker centres are a unique feature of our heartlands and in many mature towns, these often become focal points for the neighbourhood, together in the source of affordable sustenance for families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Yet, in the whole of Sengkang, there has only been one hawker centre and it is not even an NEA-run one, at least thus far.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But private control of hawker centres throws up yet another reason for expensive hawker food.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The price component will maximise the tender price while the quality component which could be weighted to take up as much as half the score includes considerations such as affordability, productivity initiatives and availability of healthy options, as shared earlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In principle, the PQM allows non-price factors to come into play.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In practice however, it is not difficult to game the system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: An entire coffee shop may have just one store that offers a single healthy option.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Or store holders may price just one so-called "loss leader" item competitively, thereby qualifying for the higher quality score, but the remainder of the items may remain expensive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I have heard anecdotes from real estate insiders that quality scores for such spaces are typically very similar which suggest the quality scores could indeed be gamed, effectively defaulting the auction to a price-based one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: More crucially, feedback from my residents suggests that healthy options are few, as are reasonably priced items, with many items priced dearly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I wonder if MND has received similar feedback, and if the Minister would be willing to share how quality will be ensured, both during auction, and on an ongoing basis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: While it is true that the higher bids are not completely forgone by the public purse – after all, they go into general revenue – this amounts to a cross-subsidy, from the residents of newer estates to the general population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: One approach is to adapt rental pricing to demand conditions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In our manifesto, the Workers' Party called for such dynamic rental: when the development is first launched, rental prices can be kept lower, prior to demand being built up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This also compensates hawkers for taking on the additional risk of being a pioneer vendor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Another strategy, which this Government has already considered and implemented in other dimensions of public policy, is to move away from the highest, or the lowest, as the case may be, to setting the sealed bid to the second price.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is a so-called Vikrey auction, so named after the academic and Nobel prize winning economist who first formally described the mechanism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In a nutshell, the top bidder in the auction still wins, but the price is set at that of the second highest bid.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I would not go into the technicalities of this approach, as to why it is desirable, but suffice it to say that auction participants will tend to reveal their true willingness to pay in such a setting, while simultaneously being resistant to a gaming of the system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Vikrey auctions have been used in a number of real world settings, including, famously, on eBay.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is also used much closer to home, for our existing Certificate of Entitlement (COE) system.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But there has been some debate on whether the grants will be capitalised in higher resale prices.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: MND has said that it has evaluated the risks and will monitor the situation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Given the potential distortionary impact of subsidies, especially when supply is inelastic, I want to repeat my suggestions in the housing debate.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For many seniors, a significant portion of their wealth lies in the value of their flats.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: HDB has come up with a number of schemes for senior to monetise their flats, including the Silver Housing Bonus for those who want to downgrade, the Lease Buyback Scheme, allowing them to rent a room to supplement their retirement income and building new 2-room Flexi flats.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As we live longer, more and more seniors may have trouble with retirement adequacy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How many have been approved, and how does this compare to MND's planning parameters?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What more can be done to increase understanding and adoption of the scheme?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Would the Minister consider further enhancements to the Lease Buyback Scheme to make it more attractive, such as increasing the cash payouts?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How will Government continue to support seniors looking to monetise their flats?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, Singapore's limited assisted living options mean seniors have few choices beyond living unassisted at home, engaging a foreign domestic helper or moving into a nursing home.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Nursing home residents in Singapore tend to stay for extended periods of five to 15 years.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In contrast, the typical nursing home stay in the United States is about two years, in part due to its more diverse aged care options like retirement villages and assisted living.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But these are expensive to construct and operate.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: HDB's Community Care Apartments (CCAs) could be a cost-effective alternative for seniors who need assisted living but are not in need of round-the-clock care.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What has been the take-up rate of CCAs so far?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What is the projected demand and how many CCAs does HDB plan to build in the next 10 years?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government could boost the availability of CCAs by purchasing and renovating existing HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This was suggested during a Roundtable organised by the Leadership Institute for Global Health Transformation and reported in The Straits times.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I heard hon Member Cheryl Chan suggesting this earlier as well.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By converting these fats into CCAs, seniors will be able to more conveniently access care services they need.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It will help scale up the provision of CCAs to more seniors and enable more of them to age in place in familiar surroundings.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Henry Kwek, take your two cuts, please.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: There have been two CCAs pilots launched thus far.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: These CCAs form an important part of our evolving senior housing policy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: First, CCA pioneer a different housing layout, and much can be learned from the lived experience versus the original stated preferences of the seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Two, because they also include the assisted living services that is packaged together, the CCAs help MND understand the willingness of seniors to pay for these services, as well as the gap in expectations, meaning the projected services versus actual needs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Third, the CCAs help the Government understand the retirement adequacy of seniors to pay for cost-of-living, medical expenses and assisted living (AL) services.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: As such, can MND share on the feedback on the CCAs, as well as MND's own assessment of this programme so far?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Chairman, as Singapore ages, capacity in our nursing homes and new senior-friendly apartments will be stretched.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Some seniors also prefer new and innovative housing types and layouts, such as group homes, share apartments with friends and extended families.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Some seniors also prefer different layouts, such as large common living areas with smaller individual rooms.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: They also look forward to retrofitting their existing homes through, maybe, improved Enhancement for Active Seniors (EASE) fittings.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: There is also an urgent need to create space within existing public and private housing estates to support in-situ assisted living (AL) services to support seniors to age-in-place.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: This is a core issue that concerns the People's Action Party (PAP) senior group.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: As such, can Minister for National Development share on the general approach in working with the whole-of-Government (WOG), especially with Ministry of Health (MOH), to reshape our existing housing estates to make ageing-in-place a reality?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Can MND share on the progress on some of these, such as the Parry Avenue site as well as any plans to update the EASE to factor in the evolving needs of seniors?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Most of these blocks had undergone the Home Improvement Programme (HIP) except for one precinct, which comprises of blocks 512 to 518 of Bedok North Avenue 2 and block 554 for Bedok North Street 3.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I understand that the said blocks were ineligible because this precinct had probably undergone a Main Upgrading Programme (MUP).

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Being part of an old HDB estate, these nine blocks have a considerable number of elderly occupants.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In my interaction with some of my elderly residents through house visits and community outreach, I received feedback requesting for the replacement of pipe sockets with new clothes drying racks.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I note that this is one of the compulsory improvements under the HIP.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These elderly residents said that they envied their friends whose flats had been installed with this feature as it makes hanging laundry less challenging.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I sincerely hope HDB will give this request some thought.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, Budget 2023 continued to pave the way towards a more inclusive and liveable Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am heartened that our young people will be better able to realise their housing aspirations and our seniors will also be better equipped to age-in-place.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In pursuit of a more inclusive Singapore, we need to continue to empower those who are vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, as a Member of the PAP senior group, I would like to draw attention to two such groups: our lower-income seniors and older women.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Against the backdrop of a rapidly ageing population, Singapore is also witnessing the feminisation of ageing, where women outlive men.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While the life expectancies of both men and women have been increasing, the life expectancy of women continues to be higher than that of men over the years.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Older women are also more likely to spend more years in disability than men, with higher reported rates of morbidity and lower mobility.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In terms of carrying out everyday activities, older women are twice as likely to report some level of difficulty as compared to men.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, we are likely to see a growing pool of older women with poorer health expectancy and who live alone, making them more vulnerable to feelings of loneliness.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, I would like to ask how many older women presently live alone in our housing estates and if there have been any attempts to understand the impact of our built environment on their socio and emotional well-being.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since the feminisation of aging is set to accelerate in coming years, what provisions have been made to cater to the needs of our older women?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Specifically, how can our neighbourhoods better enable our older women to remain socially engaged?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One suggestion can be to have more physical activity stations that are catered for women in our void decks.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These stations can focus on strength training to curb the degradation of muscle mass that contributes to lower mobility and increased rates of morbidity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Within these spaces, older women can foster deeper connections among themselves through everyday bonding and community activities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With targeted and meaningful interventions, we can enable more people to embrace ageing and experience renewed meaning and fulfilment in their silver years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: In other words, seniors look to right-size primarily because of life stage.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: But the opportunity to unlock equity in their existing flats and enhance retirement adequacy makes right-sizing an even more attractive proposition.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: What are the Ministry's plans to further support seniors looking to right-size?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Mr Chairman, I speak once more on the issue of lift upgrading for the six blocks of HDB flats in Hougang SMC where there are still certain units which do not have same floor lift access.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As this is a very real issue affecting a number of my residents, especially those with mobility needs requiring assistance to assess the stairs outside their units when they need to go out or come home, not to mention inconvenience to ambulances bringing people to the hospital and also additional charges for delivery items.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I feel pain when residents told me that their parents or grandparents had to be carried when accessing the stairs next to their unit.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Minister also said in COS 2021 in response to my previous calls, therefore blocks where the costs are still too high, it would not be prudent to offer the LUP, but the Government will continue to explore new technical methods to bring down LUP cost.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The lift access housing grant is not an option for most residents with whom I have spoken to on this issue so far.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As I have mentioned in my Budget debate speech, it is never easy to ask people to shift the different address and it is definitely not an empathetic solution.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many residents still cannot accept HDB's explanation of the issue of cost; something which could have been avoided, if HDB had tender out lift upgrading projects consisting of these blocks with problematic designs, together with the bulk of the HDB blocks with no design issues for LUP access.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope the HDB will work on this issue expeditiously to bring lift upgrading to all blocks in Singapore lacking lift access, including the remaining six blocks in Hougang so the affected residents can enjoy full lift access soon.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, as more of our HDB blocks cross the 50-year mark, we need to plan ahead to secure the resources needed for their upkeep.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As the COVID-19 pandemic has taught us supplies of materials and manpower cannot be taken for granted.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The flats in my Henderson Crescent estate, in Henderson Dawson, which were built in 1970s, are about 50 years old.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many flats there have problems, such as constant water leak and spalling concrete.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many residents there have expressed to me their desire for SERS.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Because with more information, residents will be better equipped to plan ahead their housing journey and also other housing matters.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng, take both cuts, please.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Chairman, when HDB designed and built HDB flats in the 1980s, the segmented flats were popular with some of the residents due to the additional privacy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As the residents age, many now prioritise the ability to access to the lifts on the same level over privacy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In recent years, HDB managed to install additional lift at some of the segmented blocks.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: One example is the impending Lift Upgrading Programme or LUP at block 906 and 910 of Jurong West Street 91 in Nanyang.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If HDB decides to buy back these segmented units, I do not suggest HDB to resell these segmented units back to Singaporeans, Instead, HDB could consider assigning JTC to lease out these segmented flats to younger workers who have no mobility issues.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In summary, I hope HDB will continue to find suitable solutions to build lift for the segmented blocks failing which HDB could provide an option for the owners of the segmented flats to sell them back to HDB at a reasonable price.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The Home Improvement Programme or HIP is a popular programme among the HDB owners, especially when the flats are getting older.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This means that flats that are 25 to 35 years old, are eligible for HIP.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is quite a range, thus it is not surprising that the residents staying in the older flats are expecting they should be given priority to participate in the HIP.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, we understand that the COVID-19 pandemic has slowed down the pace of HIP quite significantly.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thus, many HDB blocks above the age of 30 years were not upgraded.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In Nanyang, we have 74 blocks that are over 30 years, but there are still no HIP in sight.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The residents staying in these blocks are eagerly waiting for HIP and I hope HDB can fulfil their dream soon.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Meanwhile, I would also like to highlight that several residents have given me their feedback about the new retractable clothes-drying racks that are installed at the latest batch of HIP.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The new retractable clothes-drying rack is an improvement over the previous T-shaped design.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Many residents feedback that the new rack is not sufficiently wide to dry big sheets.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The over capacity of the new drying rack is also limited.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thus, I would like to ask if HDB has plans to improve the clothes drying rack further.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, all of us should care about biodiversity and the protection of endangered species.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I propose that we enhance our efforts in tackling the illegal wildlife trade to better reflect Singapore's role as a globally important transport node.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In last year's Endangered Species Act debate, the hon Member Mr Louis Ng asked if wildlife trafficking could be classified as a serious offence under the Organised Crime Act.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I understand that Hong Kong has passed a Bill classifying the illegal wildlife trade under a similar law they have, the Organised and Serious Crimes Ordinance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I agree with this call and would also like to ask if the agencies tasked with tackling the illegal wildlife trade could explore coordination with their counterparts in countries identified to be key originating sources for shipments of such goods.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: On the local consumption front, can I check if the Ministry engages with traditional medicine practitioners to encourage them to highlight the negative impacts from consuming endangered animal products to potential consumers?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, residents have raised concerns following some brutal cases of animal cruelty recently.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am aware it is not easy to obtain evidence in such cases.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, in my opinion, punishments are too lax.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I call on NParks to expedite its ongoing review of these penalties.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I also hope NParks will consider a complementary, restorative approach to tackling animal cruelty.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This could mean requiring abusers to attend follow-ups with psychologists.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: NParks could also use touchpoints like pet shops and veterinary clinics to explain to owners why physical punishment and other ill-treatment like chaining, confining and not walking dogs, for example, are cruel practices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Afterall, people who mistreat animals may mistreat human beings too, one day.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Chairman, there has been frequent feedback on birds causing a nuisance in our estates in Bishan and Toa Payoh.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The most recent reports are mainly of crow attacks.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Other common and longstanding complaints include bird droppings on laundry, windows and ledges, and noise nuisance created by the cawing and crowing of the birds.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: On the other hand, there are also residents who, for reasons of biodiversity, object to actions such as tree pruning, trapping and culling, to reduce the populations of crows, mynahs and pigeons.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The bird droppings cause hygiene and health concerns, affect the general aesthetics of the town and lead to higher maintenance costs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The most effective method to manage the bird population is to eliminate their shelter and food sources.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: In NParks' regular crow surveys, NParks would highlight areas in HDB estates with crows' nests to the Town Council for removal.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would it be more effective and efficient if NParks were to remove the nests instantly when spotted instead?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Could NParks increase the frequency of crow trapping and set more traps at different locations in the estates at the same time to increase the effectiveness of the actions?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Could NParks be the implementing agency on these issues, take the lead with NEA and waste collection companies to develop more effective waste disposal measures to minimise exposed food waste for birds to feed on?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Besides public education, we also need heavier penalties for bird feeding and improper waste disposal so that the offenders will be deterred from re-offending so as to be fair to other residents who have to suffer the inconveniences brought about by their actions.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: One group of residents have been severely affected by the loud crowing made by roosters regardless of day or night.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The residents may be working from home, preparing for exams, taking a rest from shift work, or elderlies who need rest.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Some have resorted to installing expensive sound-proof windows.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Others send me videos or sound files as evidence of how noisy the roosters are.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: They are unable to rest or sleep well due to the constant disturbances.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: They are deeply frustrated, despite the various measures the task force has taken.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: These include relocating some roosters, pruning trees, placing nets over trees at hotspots, an ongoing egg hunt-and-collection and public education through walkabouts and talks by my grassroots leaders, volunteers and agencies' staff about not feeding the chickens.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The other group of residents is very protective of these chickens, literally losing sleep over missing chickens.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Some residents continue to feed the chickens against our advice to let them forage naturally.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This has contributed to overpopulation and attracted other pests.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The task force strives to find a balance between having some chickens in the estate while reducing the inconveniences brought about by the overpopulation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: However, the issue has continued for far too long and has incurred too much time, effort and resources and it is therefore time to step up efforts.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Currently, the task force has to look for farms that are prepared to accept these chickens, build a cage of a suitable size to house them and with each farm only allowed to have ten chickens, this entire process cannot be an efficient solution to the situation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: We all know that feeding of chickens is a major contributor to the overpopulation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would the Ministry consider including chickens in the Wildlife Act so that those caught feeding them will be deterred by the fines?

speaker: The Chairman
text: I suspect this is the first time that chickens are featured so much in the COS.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As a matter of consistency, I am raising the issue of the keeping cats in HDB flats again this year, similar to the last few years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am speaking up because this policy of not allowing the keeping of cats just does not make any sense, we do not even enforce it and it is not fair.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: So many people are already keeping cats in HDB, so many Members of this House see our residents breaking this policy and so many people have provided legitimate and good reasons as to why this policy should change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The cats are tired of running and hiding and it is time to end this cat and mouse game.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: More than a decade ago, before I was elected as a Member of Parliament, I sat in the Animal Welfare Legislative Review Committee to review Singapore's animal welfare legislation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It has been quite some time since we last increase penalties for animal abuse and cruelty.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Stories of animal abuse have emerged in the news with worrying frequency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Several cases of animal cruelty and abuse have also come before the Court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We know for a fact that the number of animal cruelty and welfare feedback to AVS has also risen over the years.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Chairman, I would like to address the issue of public rental flats and the difficulties faced by those who do not have someone else to co-apply with for a rental unit.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Some of them will get a list of people in similar situations from HDB and try to find someone to co-apply.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: But according to them, some of these people in the list do not respond, they are not interested or they are not suitable.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: And for those who manage to find a suitable person, I have come across cases where, sometime later, they will face problems staying together and one of them will end up wanting to get the other person out of the flat.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: This scheme would accommodate those who do not have someone to apply with, or do not want to live with a stranger.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The flats could be smaller to cater to a single person.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: To ensure fairness, the rental for these flats could be higher, to justify the greater privacy that they enjoy.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Allowing this will also prevent many social problems further downstream.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Notwithstanding my proposal for the Single Singles Scheme, I do support the Joint Singles Scheme Operator-run pilot that was launched in 2021.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I believe operators would have expertise or would have built expertise to help match suitable tenants to live together and there are people who prefer living with someone for company and mutual support.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Out of the 158 units in the pilot, what number of tenants are still living together?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Have we met the objective of helping these singles with their living needs?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Moving forward, I would like to know how MND intends to proceed with the pilot.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Will this operator-run scheme be extended to more operators and locations, whether it will be further tweaked?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The problem is exacerbated because the rent a flat is small and elderly singles struggle to adapt to the different habits of another stranger.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, some of these seniors resort to living in a void deck.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For seniors who do not wish to share the flat with a stranger, they keep appealing to HDB, to be allowed to rent a flat on their own.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The amount of administrative time spent processing such appeals again and again must be massive.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What has the response been to the scheme?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And sometimes a death could have been avoided that had there been another occupant living in the same flat and who could alert emergency services to seek help.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, if a senior living alone has a heart attack or a stroke, having another person live in the same flat may mean a life saved.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In some countries where the seniors live in retirement villages, the village is marketed as a place where seniors can come together to enjoy each other's company to partake in senior friendly activities and to come together to celebrate good food as they age gracefully.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Could MND share more about the status of the Joint Singles Operator-run scheme.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Is the operator able to think innovatively to place two seniors to a flat successfully?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If so, would HDB consider expanding the pilot scheme to more sites?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I have two suggestions to strengthen its role.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As is well known, the Court is required to look into the needs of children when deciding on the division of matrimonial property.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I have seen cases where, for reasons of expediency, the husband and wife consent in Court to arrangements that run the danger of leaving the children without proper housing options.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Thereafter, one of them will appeal for urgent rental housing for them and their children, presenting HDB with a fait accompli.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In 2020, the hon Minister stated in this House that less than 10% of rental households have more than four members.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: On the ground, my sense is that there are informal arrangements which may not have been notified to HDB.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Minister also highlighted measures to help these households.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: All these are commendable but we should aim for zero overcrowding.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Each child is precious and we must do our utmost to ensure that they grow up in more conducive housing environment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I wonder if the Housing and Development Act may be reviewed to give them a proprietary interest over the purchased house even if they may not have been the registered owners.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, as part of the September 2022 set of cooling measures, the Loan-to-Value (LTV) limit for all HDB loans was further lowered from 85% to 80%, to encourage more financial prudence when taking on loans.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I agree with the Government on the need to tighten lending criteria.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I support the raising of interest rate floor used to compute mortgage servicing ratio in order to avoid overleveraging amidst a rising rate environment.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, the lowering of LTV further to 80% means 20% of cash or CPF is needed upfront for the flat purchase.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This excludes the significant expenses home buyers need to also put aside for renovation and other cost.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many first-timers have found this cash outlay substantial and difficult to afford even if they can afford to service the debt repayment based on the latest debt servicing ratio.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For example, in Hong Kong, first-time home buyers qualify for a higher loan-to-value ratio of 90%.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: But this also means that they cannot buy a replacement flat until after the divorce is finalised.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Not every divorcing couple has the option of renting another flat while waiting for the divorce to be settled and their matrimonial flat sold.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: For the party who has custody of the children and usually that is the mother.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: She is left wondering where would she and the children stay after the matrimony flat is sold.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: It would take time for them to buy another flat while waiting for the matrimony flat to be sold.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Thus, it is reasonable that the parent would want to plan ahead for the next home for the children so as to offer them some security and a roof over their heads.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: HDB can set a condition that if the matrimonial flat is not sold within six months of the interim judgment for whatever reason, then the party who had bought the replacement flat would have to surrender the flat back to HDB.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Chairman, in view of the rising demand for flats, how many new BTO flats in non-mature estates or new towns are to be built per year in the next three years?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Will these include Community Care Apartments (CCAs) which are very popular and expected to be in higher demand, flats with shorter leases and public rental flats?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Recently, we had an extensive debate on the need to keep housing affordable and to do so in a way that is fair to future generations.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, public housing in Singapore is not just about providing a home for individuals or even families.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The HDB realises many objectives including upholding our multiracial society, ensuring the family unit is kept intact, by way of proximity grants, retirement planning and saving, by way of the financial schemes.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Second, because of this, housing issues are often complex and require not just deep cognitive effort, but also knowledge of our political history.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Minister and his colleagues have already corrected some of the mistaken claims and calculations presented earlier, so I shall not repeat them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I bring these points up to show both the salience and the complexity of housing issues and to thank the many public officers in HDB and MND for their effort.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There is a larger grant for resale HDB flats, but this does not solve the problem of a tight BTO supply in the short run.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Is there a way to give some priority in the queue for these two groups?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Could the Ministry share concretely how much it expects the chance of securing a flat quickly to improve for the sub-category of first-timers that it is targeting with its latest move?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Could the Ministry update on its progress in and plans for the Comlink Rental Scheme?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Could the Ministry provide an update on the plans —

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Chair, housing accessibility has come into the forefront of national discussions in recent months.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: I am encouraged that MMD has been taking steps to boost the chances of first-time home owners.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: However, I encounter residents who are facing challenges as second timers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: For example, by changing the quantum of the resale levy or other support schemes.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Many second-timer families under the public rental scheme have also benefited from the Fresh Start Housing scheme.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Does HDB have any updates on how the recent announcements shared last year under Fresh Start have benefited residents so far?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: I was delighted to be part of the engagement which started in 2021 and it was heartening to see many Singaporeans come together to think, discuss and share ideas on how they envision our future Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
